analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain to oil and gas drilling with environmental safeguards and revenue sharing.
analysis.headline: The Senate Energy Committee reported a bill to open about 1.5 million acres of the Arctic Refuge's coastal plain to oil leasing, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have authorized companies to bid for oil and gas leases across roughly 1.5 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain, with rules requiring drilling to cause no significant harm to fish and wildlife. Half the revenue would go to Alaska, with the rest divided among conservation funds, wetlands protection, and energy research. Congress itself would have declared drilling compatible with the refuge's purpose, and the bill died without ever getting a Senate vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain access to a large, unexplored federal oil province through competitive lease sales. Alaska would receive 50 percent of leasing and royalty revenue. The Land and Water Conservation Fund, a national wetlands protection account, and energy conservation and alternative-energy research would each get dedicated shares. Alaska Native corporations holding subsurface rights in the refuge would have federal restrictions on those interests repealed [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Interior Secretary to establish a competitive oil and gas leasing program on the roughly 1.549-million-acre Coastal Plain, with lease sales capped at 300,000 acres each and an initial sale required within months of final regulations [S2][S3].
Grants leases to the highest responsible bidder with a royalty of at least 12.5 percent, and requires the public to receive fair market value for the minerals [S3].

Creates a dedicated revenue stream: 50 percent to Alaska, 20 percent to the Land and Water Conservation Fund, 15 percent to a national wetlands protection account, 10 percent to the Treasury, and 5 percent to research on energy conservation and alternative fuels [S3].

Repeals restrictions on subsurface interests held by the Inupiat Eskimo people and their corporations within the refuge, and gives their corporations expedited court treatment for any takings claims [S2][S3].

Requires strong safeguards on paper: a 'no significant adverse effect' standard for fish and wildlife, strict liability for oil spill damages, bonding, site-specific assessments, twice-yearly inspections, a 5-cent-per-barrel reclamation fund, and a ban on exporting Coastal Plain crude oil [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Arctic Refuge itself: a pristine Arctic ecosystem — caribou calving grounds, snow goose habitat, and subsistence hunting areas used by local Native communities — would host exploration rigs, ice roads, pipelines, and production facilities, with any 'no significant adverse effect' guarantee depending on regulators keeping that promise. The public would also give up the option of keeping the refuge undeveloped, and the environmental risk would fall on fish, wildlife, and subsistence users rather than on the companies holding the leases [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: The refuge ecosystem and subsistence users

drawbacks.text: Congress itself — not the Interior Secretary — would declare that oil and gas activities 'compatible' with the refuge's purpose as long as they cause no significant adverse effect, and it would deem the controversial 1987 environmental impact statement legally adequate, removing normal environmental review of the decision to open the refuge [S2][S3].

The coastal plain is the calving ground of the Porcupine caribou herd and critical habitat for snow geese and other species; even the bill's own structure — facilities, pipelines, winter exploration — accepts permanent industrial presence in a wildlife refuge in exchange for revenue [S3].

The bill contains a non-severability clause: if courts invalidated the 50 percent revenue share to Alaska, the entire leasing program would be void, a provision that tied the whole scheme's fate to a revenue allocation expected to draw legal challenge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine compromise: it pairs drilling with unusually detailed environmental mandates, strict liability, and new funding for conservation and alternative energy. But the fundamental trade is unchanged — a one-time industrial development of the nation's largest remaining Arctic wilderness in exchange for revenue and a 'no significant harm' promise that only long-term regulation could test. For anyone who values the refuge as a refuge, the costs are permanent and the revenue is finite.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Energy Committee wrote and reported the bill itself and put it on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: The Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee ordered an original bill reported on March 16, 1989, in place of an earlier ANWR leasing bill (S. 406) [S5].

Committee chairman J. Bennett Johnston reported the bill to the Senate on March 29, 1989, with written report 101-10; additional and minority views were filed alongside it, signaling disagreement within the committee [S5].
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 34, waiting for floor time [S3][S5].
No senator cosponsored the bill [S4], and no further action was ever taken; the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Those who wanted the Arctic Refuge's coastal plain left undeveloped: the area remained closed to oil leasing, and the oil industry got no leases and no revenue.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call vote was ever taken, no senator cosponsored the bill, and the committee report carried additional and minority views, so the partisan split cannot be measured from the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would open a closed federal wildlife refuge to competitive leasing, giving oil companies access to a major untapped province while the public bears the environmental risk. The industry's gain is the refuge's loss of protected status [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Alaska Native regional corporations (Arctic Slope Regional Corporation, Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation)
industries.note: The bill repeals federal restrictions on their subsurface oil and gas interests inside the refuge and gives them expedited courts for takings claims, letting them profit from development on their lands. Local subsistence users in the same communities could lose hunting and fishing resources to drilling activity [S3].

industries.industry: Recreation, tourism, and subsistence users of the Arctic Refuge
industries.note: Industrial access roads, pipelines, and drilling operations in the coastal plain would directly conflict with the wilderness character and subsistence hunting that these users depend on. The bill requires only that impacts on subsistence uses be avoided 'to the extent practicable' [S3].
